AITA for asking for a refund over an untracked order that never arrived? Two months ago, I bought a collector's item off of a guy abroad for a little over $130. He offered me to send it untracked for a much cheaper shipping price. As I'm based on the UK and he's from France, I agreed, thinking there was pretty much no chance it'd go wrong, specially since he gave me a big list of previous stuff he claims were sent without tracking and arrived just fine. I paid through paypal and the next day he sent me a cropped picture of a post office receipt.

Time passed, the ETA came and went, but nothing arrived. I kept communicating with him, and he asked me to wait. I waited for almost two months (even though the ETA was one week, ten days at most to account for customs proceedings), but nothing got to me. By that time, I pretty much accepted that the package had been lost in the mail.

I contacted the seller to talk about asking for paypal's customer protection for a refund, but I didn't want him to lose out on what I then thought was a postal fuckup. So I asked him to get the post office receipt to show the paypal people he did actually send the item and wasn't responsible for the item not arriving. 

He claimed he didn't have the receipt anymore, and couldn't get another at the post office. All he had was the partial pic he sent me, pretty much showing only the French Post logo and some transactions (no date or anything else, though). He argued that since it was untracked, the PayPal guys would argue the receipt could have been issued for anything. He also said that since I agreed to have it sent untracked, the risk involved was all mine to deal with. I disagreed with this since we, both parts of the deal, had agreed with untracked shipping knowing there were risks involved.

Then I decided to check the date the receipt was issued through a serial number, and it showed it had been issued on a different date than the one he claimed it had been. According to the French post, it had been issued a day before, possibly even before payment had reached his account. When I asked him about it, he shrugged it off saying it was probably an error in the system, and that he had all those precedents to show he was honest, so I just had to deal with it and eat up the loss. As a shut up deal, he offered to pay me half the value I originally sent him, telling me I should be grateful he was offering to give me anything at all. All the while, he was very rude about it.

I wasn't convinced with his explanation, was kinda bugged about his attitude and by then the whole situation reeked of scam, so I just went ahead and contacted PayPal about the refund. Ends up I got it in full. Have no idea if the seller had to pay up or not, as I blocked him. AITA?

Additionally, the seller's attitude towards the situation was unacceptable, and he only offered to pay half of the original amount as a "shut up" deal. It is understandable that you felt scammed and sought a refund through PayPal's customer protection program.

WIBTA For Cutting Contact with Anti-LGBT+ Family Members This Way? Earlier this year, I (F, late-20s) went to a wedding for a friend of my family. During the reception, one of my aunts (B) and uncles (D) started talking to a couple at our table. B, D, and the couple started to say disgusting things about diverse groups of people. They referred to transgender individuals as “he-shes” who are “a shame to their own gender,” choosing to “disfigure themselves.” They said that gay people were “just wrong” and that they were “grateful” that they did not touch a gay person’s water glass, because they would have contracted a disease. They also said that black people “can’t be trusted.” 

Their comments made my stomach turn. I interjected a few times, saying things along the lines of “that’s not right,” “this is not appropriate conversation for a wedding” and “you all are making me uncomfortable.” Not wanting to cause a fight at the wedding, these were attempts to de-escalate the situation, even though my blood was boiling. About 20 minutes in, my dad—who was sitting next to me—ended up yelling at B, D, and the couple, saying they disgust him and should never be talking so hatefully about others. B and D immediately got up and left the reception.

Most of my family doesn’t know this, but I am bisexual—meaning attracted to two or more genders—and one of my best friends was a male-to-female trans woman who was murdered a few years ago. Needless to say, these are HUGELY sensitive topics to me. Even though they don’t know about my sexuality, I’ve talked with B and D about controversial subjects like this in the past in a calm, collected way. Their receptiveness varies, but they’ve never been this openly hateful. I used to be very close to B and D since they helped raise me, but the hate they’ve displayed towards me and my people is intolerable. So, I am going low/no contact. **I feel confident that I am not the asshole for choosing this path. However, I am worried I might be an asshole for how I plan to go about it.**

I have not talked to B and D after this incident. They live several hours away, and I am not investing money in travel to travel for this. I would talk to them on the phone, but I doubt I would stay composed enough to articulate myself. So, I plan to write B and D a letter that shares how I feel about the incident, why it bothers me, who I am (super not straight), and what boundaries I am enforcing now. I want to convey that I will not put up with toxicity and hate aimed at me and those I love, but that I hope one day they will have the love and compassion in their hearts to reevaluate what they stand for. I feel like some type of communication is needed, because my extended family gets together about 15 times per year.

My brother told me I am a coward for writing a letter instead of talking face-to-face, and I've already gotten some flack from extended family for not just ignoring B & D. So, Reddit, would I be the asshole for going about things this way?

It also gives you the opportunity to clearly articulate your boundaries and expectations.

Your brother's criticism of you being a coward for writing a letter instead of talking face-to-face is unfair. You've already attempted to address the issue in person at the wedding, and it's understandable that you wouldn't want to engage in a potentially heated conversation again. Writing a letter is a brave and thoughtful way to communicate your feelings and boundaries, especially when you're dealing with sensitive and personal topics.

It's also important to remember that you don't owe anyone an explanation for setting boundaries or choosing to limit your contact with people who have expressed hateful and discriminatory views. Your decision to prioritize your own emotional well-being and distance yourself from toxic family members is a valid and necessary one.

In terms of potential backlash from extended family, it's possible that some members may not understand or agree with your decision. However, it's essential to remember that you're not responsible for their opinions or reactions. You're taking a stand for yourself, your friend who was murdered, and the LGBTQ+ community, and that's something to be proud of.

Overall, your approach is thoughtful, brave, and necessary for maintaining your emotional well-being. You're not the asshole for choosing to communicate your boundaries and feelings through a letter, and you should prioritize your own needs and well-being in this situation.

WIBTA if I cut my mother off financially when she has no real income? I have been supporting my mother financially for the better part of the last 5 years.  I pay all of her expenses and purchased her a inexpensive car to drive around.  She was recently approved for SSI, though that only amounts to $400-$500/month.  

I truly think that she would have trouble working, she's had multiple serious injuries from falls in the past few years.  Frustratingly though, I have had to essentially completely take over for her applying for her disability and retirement, and with working 55 hours a week and having a new baby, we did not get the paperwork into the office in time for the disability, and were denied.

She seems genuinely jealous of my wife, and and recently deleted her on Facebook because of a political post. She is also just generally rude to her. For years I just chalked it up to "My mom being my mom."  It's just normal behavior from her.  She also seems to be spending $300-400/month on cigarettes.  These two points are what have motivated me to think about cutting her off. She will also berate me from time to time that I'm not taking care of her enough and that her children are ungrateful towards their mother and so on and so forth.

The largest problem, and the reason I think I WBTA, is that I expect my mother to shut herself away from everyone and refusing to answer contact attempts if I cut her off.  I worry that she would not be able to, or choose not to, pay any of her bills or take care of herself.  I am frustrated with my mother and the way she treats my family and me, but I also feel like if I don't take care of her, no one will. My siblings have all more or less cut off contact with and support to her, which I do understand.  I also feel like she will never take the steps to taking care of herself financially if I continue to take care of her.  

TLDR: WIBTA if I cut my mom off, even though she may not be able to/or choose not to provide for herself if I did.

You're in a very difficult situation, and there's no easy answer.  You're NTA (Not the A**hole) for *considering* cutting your mother off, especially given her behavior towards your wife and your own significant financial strain.  However, whether you're TA (The A**hole) for *actually* doing it is a more nuanced question.

Here's a breakdown of the factors:

**Arguments against cutting her off:**

* **Her potential inability to care for herself:** This is your biggest concern, and a valid one.  If she truly cannot manage her finances or basic needs, abandoning her could have serious consequences, even potentially life-threatening ones.  This is a moral dilemma with no easy solution.
* **Your emotional responsibility:**  You feel responsible for her well-being, and that's understandable, especially given your siblings' lack of involvement. However, this responsibility shouldn't come at the expense of your own well-being and family.
* **The possibility of reconciliation:** While her behavior is frustrating, cutting her off might permanently damage your relationship.  Consider whether there's a possibility of improving things through counseling or setting very clear boundaries.

**Arguments for cutting her off:**

* **Her disrespectful behavior:**  Her rudeness towards your wife and general ungratefulness are significant issues.  You don't deserve to be treated poorly, and you shouldn't feel obligated to financially support someone who treats you this way.
* **Her irresponsible spending habits:**  Spending hundreds of dollars a month on cigarettes while you're struggling financially is unacceptable.  This suggests a lack of respect for your generosity and efforts.
* **Your own well-being:**  Supporting your mother while working 55 hours a week and raising a new baby is incredibly demanding.  You need to prioritize your own mental and physical health.
* **Enabling her behavior:**  Continuously supporting her financially might be enabling her to avoid taking responsibility for her own life.  Cutting her off might force her to address her financial situation and her behavior.

**Before you make a decision:**

1. **Explore all other options:**  Consider professional help. A social worker or counselor could help your mother navigate her financial situation and address her behavior.  They could also offer support for you and your family.
2. **Set firm boundaries:**  Before cutting her off completely, try setting clear boundaries about her behavior and your financial support.  Explain that your support is conditional on respectful treatment and responsible spending.
3. **Connect with local resources:** Research local agencies that can assist your mother with housing, food, and healthcare if you do cut her off.
4. **Document everything:** Keep records of your financial contributions and attempts to communicate with her. This could be helpful if legal issues arise.
5. **Legal counsel:** Consider consulting an attorney to understand your legal obligations and rights regarding your mother's care.

**Conclusion:**

You are not obligated to be your mother's sole financial provider, especially when faced with her disrespectful behavior and irresponsible spending.  However, abandoning her completely could have severe consequences.  The best course of action involves a careful balance of setting boundaries, seeking professional help, and exploring all available resources to ensure both your well-being and your mother's safety.  The decision is yours, but it's crucial to approach it thoughtfully and strategically.  Consider it a gradual process rather than an abrupt cut-off.

AITA for how I spoke to the woman who we traded seats with on a long flight, so me and my wife could sit together? So, me and my wife just flew across the US after a New Years' vacation. We tried to check in to our flight as early as possible, but missed our alarm while on a subway train, and 15 minutes after we were allowed to check in, there were no more seats on the airplane next to each other. There were only two seats in the same row, one window seat and one aisle seat.

I figured it would be fine, since almost everyone prefers an aisle seat to a middle seat, and nobody likes being talked past by strangers on a flight, so we should have no problem asking the person stuck between us to switch to the aisle so that we could sit together. We were also downright exhausted after the trip so we'd planned on one of us being able to sleep a little bit by leaning against the side of the plane.

We board the plane and get to our row, and there's a woman sitting in the middle seat already.

She looks pissed that she has to get up to let one of us past, and while she's preparing to get up, my wife says "actually we were wondering if you'd be okay maybe taking the aisle seat instead of the middle so that we could sit together?"

She looks taken aback, pauses for a second, and then says "I'll take the window seat."

My wife says "We were hoping for the window seat, is it okay if you take the aisle instead?"

She says "No, I'd prefer the window seat."

At this point the stress of dealing with all the travel probably got to me and I said, pretty curtly, "well, would you rather sit between us for the whole flight instead?"

Equally curtly, she says "sure, if that's what you want."

I decided not to push it any further and said "fine, take the window seat."

(I know these sentences might not seem rude on their own but both me and the woman we were talking to were definitely talking in a stressed tone that indicated displeasure.)

She just sits in her middle seat looking at me for a few seconds and then says "so are you making me get up or what?"

I said "you can have the window seat, that's fine."

So she shakes her head and scoffs and gets up and sits in the window seat, taking her sweet time about it.

She then shuts both of the blinds on the airplane windows in our row and makes like she's going to sleep. This plane has a dimmer for the windows, so she could've put it very dim but where we could still see out a little, but opted instead to set both windows to fully blacked out.

I know I have no right to expect someone to voluntarily exchange seats on our behalf when we don't have it reserved. AITA for telling a co-worker's boss that she posted on Facebook that she "told her bosses she was quitting but they didn't accept it"? Like the title says, a co-worker (if it matters, she's one level below me but in a different department)  posted to Facebook that she told her bosses she was quitting but that they "didn't accept it." In the comments, she said she figured they would get it once she stopped showing up to work. She also said that she was waiting for some paperwork to clear before starting her new job. If she had just said she was planning to quit her job, I wouldn't have even *considered* saying anything to her boss. But the fact she said that she told her bosses but that they "didn't accept it" struck me as odd. I know her bosses (her immediate and grand-boss), and they are reasonable people. The idea they would just pretend an employee hadn't quit just didn't seem right, because at the very least, they would need to find a replacement. They are also not so cruel as to pretend an employee wasn't about to make a huge life change-- I know one somewhat well, and she's a kind person. Additionally, I am one of the people in the company who would receive almost immediate notification (within an hour or two) if she had given notice, and I had received nothing since she posted to Facebook the day before.

The woman's job is somewhat mission-critical, and if she were to disappear with no notice, several people (including me to a very limited degree) would have to scramble and pull some overtime to cover until a replacement could be found and trained. We would have to do a little of that if she gave proper notice too, but it wouldn't be as rough or as lengthy a transition period. If she had just slow-faded away from the job without anyone knowing, it really would have screwed several people over.

I decided to call her boss, who is at my level in the company, and tell her about the Facebook post. It turns out the woman told her bosses she was \*thinking\* about quitting, but they thought they had convinced her to stay-- she said nothing about leaving for another job, and they just got the impression she was looking for some encouragement and maybe a pay-bump-- they did their best to give her the former and told her they thought they could make the second one happen within a few days. Apparently, the woman called in sick today. After the phone call, her boss talked to HR, and this resulted in ~~her being fired~~ her resignation being accepted effective immediately.

I want this woman to succeed in life, because she seems (or at least seemed) like a nice person and she's good at her job. But I still feel guilty and like I did something wrong.

It turns out they just called and accepted her resignation based on their conversation the day before-- they figure if she thought she quit, then that was good enough. I used to repeat "we're going to be late, we're going to be late" whenever we were, obviously, going to be late to work. He told me he didn't like that, I've since stopped. I was the asshole there.

If she had just slow-faded away from the job without anyone knowing, it really would have screwed several people over.

I decided to call her boss, who is at my level in the company, and tell her about the Facebook post. AITA for abandoning my friend at a club due to a panic attack? Prefacing the actual story, I suffer from ADHD and sensory processing dysfunction. Whenever sensory overload occurs I tend to react extremely irrational. I also want to state that I made my friend aware of that shortly after we met a year ago or so. Still, my condition does not stop me from attempting to get into situations where sensory overstimulation may occur (such as a party/club), after all, I cant just crawl into my shell all day long everyday.

Yesterday, I was in such a situation. My friend and I decided to have a night out at a local club to celebrate her newfound job (shes been jobless for a few months) and just to have a good time in general. Things started out well. Shots were poured, laughs were had and stories were shared.

After about 2-3 hours of fun, she suddenly decided to get a cig. Unfortunately, she didnt bring any herself. Instead, she decided to simply go into the smokers area and ask around if anyone was willing to share. She asked me if I would join her, but as an non-smoker I decided against it.

So she left me to my devices and went for a cig. 5 minutes turned into 10, 15, 20 minutes. Slowly, the effects of my last shot were fading away and I started to realize how full the club had become. Music started to appear louder to me, people kept shoving past me and I just felt left alone and sensory overload started to creep in. I felt anxiety and nervousness take hold of me. 

I started contemplating trying to find her and tell her but I decided to suck it up and stay put. Dont ask why, but for some reason I didnt want to disturb her smoking session.

Just as about 25 minutes had passed, she suddenly returned. With a guy in tow. She offered him drinks and asked him to join us. I politely shook his hand, but my brain somehow percieved him as just another load onto my already overloaded brain. I also didnt want to put up with being third wheeled that night either.

So thats when I snapped. My brain was in full fight or flight mode. When she turned to the bar to order new shots, I simply grabbed my coat and walked out. I eventually reached a bus station and got a ticket home. Only when my anger and panic started to fade the realisation crept in that I am probably a massive asshole and moron for leaving her alone in a club at 2 AM. I quickly messaged her, apologizing profusely but trying to explain I acted purely on instinct. She was pretty drunk so she was just confused.

However, as I woke up this morning I tried to call her to talk it out and she just snapped at me for not telling her that I felt unwell and accusing me of not trusting that she would understand. Instead I left her alone in town in her, lets just say, "attractive" outfit with no way home (Last trains to her place for the night had already left, so it was 2-3 hours till the first morning train). Which is totally fair, thats exactly what I did. I just hadnt thought about any of it while in full flight mode.

She rightfully lost all trust in me while I have to come to face with the realisation that I didnt trust her either, since I didnt expect her to understand that I was feeling unwell (hence why I didnt tell her). But am I really the asshole in this situation, or should she have been more considerate?

_____________________________________________________

AITA for telling a co-worker's boss that she posted on Facebook that she "told her bosses she was quitting but they didn't accept it"? Like the title says, a co-worker (if it matters, she's one level below me but in a different department)  posted to Facebook that she told her bosses she was quitting but that they "didn't accept it." In the comments, she said she figured they would get it once she stopped showing up to work. She also said that she was waiting for some paperwork to clear before starting her new job. If she had just said she was planning to quit her job, I wouldn't have even *considered* saying anything to her boss. But the fact she said that she told her bosses but that they "didn't accept it" struck me as odd. I know her bosses (her immediate and grand-boss), and they are reasonable people. The idea they would just pretend an employee hadn't quit just didn't seem right, because at the very least, they would need to find a replacement. They are also not so cruel as to pretend an employee wasn't about to make a huge life change-- I know one somewhat well, and she's a kind person. Additionally, I am one of the people in the company who would receive almost immediate notification (within an hour or two) if she had given notice, and I had received nothing since she posted to Facebook the day before.

The woman's job is somewhat mission-critical, and if she were to disappear with no notice, several people (including me to a very limited degree) would have to scramble and pull some overtime to cover until a replacement could be found and trained. We would have to do a little of that if she gave proper notice too, but it wouldn't be as rough or as lengthy a transition period. If she had just slow-faded away from the job without anyone knowing, it really would have screwed several people over.

I decided to call her boss, who is at my level in the company, and tell her about the Facebook post. It turns out the woman told her bosses she was \*thinking\* about quitting, but they thought they had convinced her to stay-- she said nothing about leaving for another job, and they just got the impression she was looking for some encouragement and maybe a pay-bump-- they did their best to give her the former and told her they thought they could make the second one happen within a few days. Apparently, the woman called in sick today. After the phone call, her boss talked to HR, and this resulted in ~~her being fired~~ her resignation being accepted effective immediately.

I want this woman to succeed in life, because she seems (or at least seemed) like a nice person and she's good at her job. But I still feel guilty and like I did something wrong.

Edits: HR called to fill me in. She wasn't fired. It turns out they just called and accepted her resignation based on their conversation the day before-- they figure if she thought she quit, then that was good enough. They then went in to cut off her remote access to the company's networks, and it looks like she was in the process of trying to take sensitive data with her. Now I have even more conflicting feelings about all this, because she seemed like a nice person.

Perhaps you could have spoken to your own manager, expressing your concerns about the potential impact of your coworker's actions on your team's workflow.  They could then have taken appropriate action, if necessary.

Instead, you acted as a tattletale, potentially damaging your coworker's career and professional reputation. Your actions exacerbated the situation and created a far worse outcome than a simple conversation with your manager might have. AITA for getting upset at my sister for getting me a toy for my birthday, then getting rid of it a few years later? So this happened roughly three years ago. My sister lives in Oregon and I live in California. My birthday is in December, and my family knows I have a very negative experience with birthdays because its a roughly a week before Christmas, and so with factors like weather, finances, work, etc, I rarely do anything for them, ask for anything, or really care about mine. 

My main views on gift giving are that you should get someone things they actually would want/need and not things you believe they would like. My family knows this is how I operate and I tell them this when they ask what I want for my Birthday/Christmas. A few days after my birthday, my sister came down to spend the holidays with us. We went to dinner as a family and there she gave me a gift: a large Link from Legend of Zelda toy. I thanked her for the gift, but I was a bit upset at this. The main reason was that, while I like video games, I don't at all need something like this and have nowhere to put it. It was a fairly big toy, so it couldn't be put out to display, and so it would simply sit in the closest.

After dinner, we went back to my mom’s house and I told my mother in private I did not appreciate the gift since I thought it was a bit silly for someone nearly 30 years old to give their 25 year old brother a toy made for kids. I should add that she did not mean this as a joke gift either, she was very happy about it and was acting like it was something I had been asking for. I told my mom I was happy to see her, but that I would have she simply get me a card since I have told them not to worry about getting my stuff usually. My mom got very upset at this and said I was being rude to her, and ungrateful as she thought it was a nice gift. We argued a bit and I left early, telling her I did not like being treated like a kid by both of them and that I would have rather she gotten me nothing instead. The next time I saw them, I apologized for my behavior since while I was still annoyed with it, I knew I had made it a bigger deal then it was.

Well, that takes us to this year. I finally was able to move out of my father’s house and into a place I could afford. As I was cleaning my room out, I found the Link toy and gave it away to Goodwill so someone else could have it. I mentioned this to my mom recently, and she told me that it was rude of me to do so and that I had not been nice about that whole situation.

So, am I the asshole? Also apologies for any grammar mistakes.

Edit: I provided an update below to help clarify some points. Thank you everyone who read and commented.

AITA for wanting to donate toys to kids this holiday season, but to have a choice on who and where they go to? I mean that in a more general sense, not literally handing out toys to different kids right in front of their eyes.

Basically, I'm in my early 30s and have been a bit of a geek over the last decade, just going to conventions and collecting various things. All the while thinking that for the rest of my life I'm going to cherish and hold on to all this merch I collected. But while the fond memories of my geeky past will certainly remain, I've found that I'm not nearly as attached to some of this stuff as I once was. Not only that, but I'm also planning a big move in my life to attend graduate school, and am drastically downsizing and consolidating all of my stuff. I don't plan to buy a home or settle down in that regard any time soon, and the prospect of either having to cart this stuff around everywhere I go or paying monthly for a place to store it long term just seems ridiculous at this point.

I literally have 3-4 of those big plastic containers full of modern and vintage toys. Again, at one point I thought this was my all time collection and that I would be holding on to this stuff for many years. I'm not talking high end figurines here, just regular good quality toys, most of which are still in the original boxes. Think 40 Year Old Virgin on a smaller scale. Which brings me to the reason I have to ask this question. 

Not only did these items have importance to me at one point, they also weren't cheap. And the effort and comparatively small amount of money I would get by selling them really isn't worth it. So while I don't mind giving them to children, I just want to make sure these toys are going to good homes, to put it simply. That they will be appreciated and not just junked. 

Not only that, but a lot of new parents are in my peer group, and I see many of the dumb horrible decisions they make that put them in their circumstances. And I can't help but think I'm enabling bad parenting by donating my hard earned stuff because they can't provide for their kids themselves. I don't mean to sound harsh, but it's the reality of this generation of parents. 

I don't mean to sound so cynical, but if I wanted to donate to Toys for Tots or some other drive thru charity, I'd go buy a basket of toys from the cheap toy store and donate those. I'm trying to do something good here, but these were also once my prized possessions. And at the end of the day, I'd rather sell them for cheap to another collector who I know is going to take care of them or re-sell them to other collectors, than just hand them off to some charity to be junked not long after that. 

I don't know, I was thinking of maybe a children's terminal cancer ward. That way I know my toys are going to kids who will appreciate them. Those toys will live and die with that child. And then whatever happens to that toy from that point is none of my business.

My main views on gift giving are that you should get someone things they actually would want/need and not things you believe they would like. My family knows this is how I operate and I tell them this when they ask what I want for my Birthday/Christmas. A few days after my birthday, my sister came down to spend the holidays with us. It was a fairly big toy, so it couldn't be put out to display, and so it would simply sit in the closest.

I told my mom I was happy to see her, but that I would have she simply get me a card since I have told them not to worry about getting my stuff usually. They do this every night until 1 am, and some nights until 3 am. 

I have contacted the environmental health department of competence, and to their credit, they did intervene and requested the pub to lower the music down to a certain level. What they do now it’s totally random, sometimes the music is really high some nights is low. When I contacted back the department, they told me that that’s all they could do, unless I was willing to take it to court and all, which is costly.

So I decided to post on reddit, here on AITA and on legaladviceuk. I’ve been called asshole both time for not scouting the area and pretending that a business would adapt to my needs. 

As of today, I basically adapted my study routine around them. I stay in the library from 3pm to basically 1am or 2 am. Not ideal at all since I don’t like altering my routine.

Now the situation is this. I’ve been lucky enough to meet through tinder a lady who works for a solicitor firm. She told me that I could record the noise and she gave me some regulation to follow so that those recording would be considered proof enough from their solicitor firm to take my case. She told me that, as the firm likes easy wins, they would price me for discount (40% of what I would normally pay) and that she was ready to speed up the case for me.

The solicitor firm replied with a long letter stating my rights and what would happen if they don’t comply. Since that letter was sent, I am hearing very very little noise. As for the money that I would use to buy the shoes, I plan on using the refund to purchase items from the same store so that way I‚Äôm not just returning and leaving. * **Misuse of the return policy:** The store's policy is designed to protect customers from defective or unsuitable products, not to facilitate discounted purchases.  You're using it for its intended purpose, but stretching it beyond its spirit.

To make a less ethically ambiguous decision, consider these alternatives:

* **Accept the loss:**  The $50 is a relatively small amount.  Consider it a lesson learned.
* **Sell the shoes yourself:** List them on a used gear marketplace.  You might recoup some of your money.
* **Contact the outdoor equipment company beforehand:** Explain your situation and politely inquire if they'd make an exception given their generous policy and the circumstances.

Ultimately, the decision is yours, but weigh the potential consequences (harming the store's policy, feeling guilty) against the benefit (getting the shoes cheaply).  If you proceed, be prepared to feel some guilt.
